title: Swords into ploughshares (Isaiah 2:4)
hook: nations shall not learn war any more

segments.voice: Yesterday, a sign for a frightened king: a child called Emmanuel. Your line was god with us. When did you say it under your breath? Day four hundred seventeen.

In the garden of the United Nations in New York there's a bronze statue of a muscular man swinging a hammer. In one hand he holds a sword, and he's bending its blade into the curved shape of a plough. It was a gift from the Soviet Union in 1959, at the height of the Cold War, which is its own kind of irony. And the idea it shows is about twenty-seven centuries old. It comes from the prophet Isaiah, from a vision so stubborn and so hopeful that both superpowers could stand in front of it and want it. Today's word is that vision.
screen: `A BRONZE MAN WITH A HAMMER.` → `A GIFT IN THE COLD WAR.` → `AN IDEA TWENTY-SEVEN CENTURIES OLD.`

segments.voice: Isaiah sees a day when the mountain of the Lord's house is lifted above every hill, and the nations stream to it. Not marched there. Streaming, the way rivers flow, except uphill. And the people say to each other: come, let us go up to the mountain of the Lord, and he will teach us his ways. Then the line. In the Douay-Rheims: "they shall turn their swords into ploughshares, and their spears into sickles: nation shall not lift up sword against nation." And the verse ends: "neither shall they be exercised any more to war." Most English speakers know that last line in another wording: they shall not learn war any more. Picture what that takes. A sword is iron. So is the blade of a plough. Same metal, reshaped. Isaiah doesn't imagine weapons vanishing. He imagines them being hammered, by hand, into tools that feed people. The energy that went into killing goes into harvest. And notice the order. First the nations come to learn God's ways. Then God settles their disputes. Then they beat their swords. Peace in this vision isn't just a ceasefire. It comes from learning a different way to live. The same words appear almost exactly in the prophet Micah. And the prophet Joel turns them inside out in a call to battle: beat your ploughshares into swords. The Bible knows both directions are possible. The Catholic Church opens Advent with this reading in one year of the cycle, and Pope John the Twenty-Third's letter Pacem in Terris, Peace on Earth, written in 1963, carried the same hope into the nuclear age.
screen: `THE NATIONS STREAM UPHILL.` · `SAME IRON, RESHAPED.` · `FIRST LEARN, THEN BEAT THE SWORDS.` · `JOEL TURNS IT INSIDE OUT.` · then, large: `NATION SHALL NOT LIFT UP SWORD AGAINST NATION.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: end one small war in your life. Settle, and breathe. Everyone has one. A cold standoff with a sibling. A running argument at work. A comment thread you keep going back to. A grudge you've been sharpening for years. Name yours. Now picture the sword in your hands: the remark you keep ready, the silence you use as a weapon. And picture hammering it, slowly, into something useful. A question instead of an accusation. A first step instead of waiting for theirs. If you pray, you can ask for help to put it down. The bell holds the time.
cherev. Hebrew for sword, the weapon Isaiah pictures nations reshaping into farm tools, because they have learned God's ways and will not learn war any more. Today's word.
Your line: ploughshares. Today, take one concrete step to end your small war: a message, a question, an apology, or just stopping the next jab. Day four hundred seventeen.

howItsDone: Catholics hear Isaiah's vision of peace on the First Sunday of Advent in one year of the Lectionary, and the Church's teaching on peace, from Pacem in Terris onward, returns to it often.

fork.setup: you're one of the nations in Isaiah's vision. you've come up the mountain and been taught God's ways. what happens next?
options: you sign a treaty and keep your swords.
you beat your swords into ploughshares.
you go home and teach others to fight better.
fork.reveal: after learning God's ways and having their disputes settled, they reshape their weapons into tools, and learn war no more.

original.note: Hebrew: sword. In Isaiah's vision the cherev is beaten into a tool for the field.

trapdoor: what you thought: a nice slogan about world peace.
what it means: nations first learn God's ways, then hammer their own weapons into tools that feed people. peace that changes how people live.
what a scholar hears: the oracle appears in both Isaiah 2 and Micah 4, and Joel 3 deliberately reverses it; scholars still debate which prophet had it first.
recall: won the hearts of Israel at the gate

notes: UN sculpture 'Let Us Beat Swords into Plowshares' by Evgeniy Vuchetich, a gift of the USSR in 1959: confirm. 'Twenty-seven centuries old' assumes Isaiah c. 8th century BC.
Joel's reversal is Joel 3:10 in the Douay and KJV (4:10 in Hebrew numbering).
Isaiah 2:1–5 is the first reading for the First Sunday of Advent, Year A; confirm.
Pacem in Terris does not quote Isaiah 2:4 directly as far as the writer knows; the script says only it 'carried the same hope'. Confirm.
The index spells 'ploughshares' (British/Douay); kept exactly as the index word and carry.
